questions.stem: A parent asks how to explain a grandparent's death to a 5-year-old child. Which guidance is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use clear, honest, developmentally appropriate language because a young child's understanding of death differs from an adult's understanding.","B":"Use the same abstract explanation given to adults because children generally understand permanence and universality of death by age 5.","C":"Avoid discussing the death because talking about loss with young children generally causes more psychological harm than supportive explanation.","D":"Tell the child the person is sleeping because euphemisms are the preferred way to prevent confusion in preschool-aged children."}}
questions.rationale: Children's understanding of death changes with age and developmental stage. NCI's PDQ grief resource notes that children roughly ages 2 to 6 may view death as temporary or sleep-like, so communication should be clear, honest, and developmentally appropriate rather than relying on adult-level abstractions or misleading euphemisms.
questions.source_name: National Cancer Institute / NCBI Bookshelf — Grief, Bereavement, and Loss (PDQ)
questions.source_detail: Children at different developmental stages understand death differently; young children may not yet understand finality and require developmentally appropriate communication.

questions.stem: A parent asks whether aspirin should be given to a 10-year-old with fever during a suspected viral illness. Which response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid aspirin in children and adolescents with suspected viral illness because of the association with Reye syndrome","B":"Use aspirin as the preferred first-line antipyretic because viral illness does not alter its pediatric safety profile","C":"Double the usual aspirin dose because higher dosing reduces the risk of neurologic complications during influenza","D":"Aspirin is appropriate whenever fever exceeds 38.5°C because the Reye-syndrome warning applies only to adults"}}
questions.rationale: Aspirin and other salicylate-containing products should generally be avoided in children and adolescents during influenza, varicella, or other suspected viral illness because of the association with Reye syndrome. The original item was tightened to avoid making an unnecessary blanket claim about specific substitute antipyretics.
questions.source_name: FDA — Required Warning for Aspirin-Containing Drug Products
questions.source_detail: Pediatric viral-illness warning regarding Reye syndrome

questions.stem: An adult has a deep contaminated puncture wound and an unknown tetanus vaccination history. Which prophylaxis should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine plus tetanus immune globulin, along with appropriate wound care","B":"Systemic antibiotics alone because antibiotics replace tetanus vaccination and immune globulin after contaminated wounds","C":"Wound cleansing alone because an unknown vaccination history is treated as proof of a complete primary series","D":"No tetanus prophylaxis unless clinical tetanus develops because puncture wounds are classified as clean minor wounds"}}
questions.rationale: CDC classifies penetrating or puncture wounds as dirty or major wounds. For a dirty or major wound with unknown vaccination history, tetanus vaccination is indicated and TIG is also indicated. Antibiotics are not recommended solely to prevent tetanus.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus
questions.source_detail: Dirty/major wound prophylaxis with unknown vaccination history

questions.stem: Which instruction is correct for use of an epinephrine auto-injector during anaphylaxis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Inject into the anterolateral thigh and follow the specific device instructions for activation and hold time","B":"Inject into the abdomen because abdominal tissue provides the recommended emergency absorption site","C":"Avoid use through clothing under all circumstances because clothing always prevents delivery of epinephrine","D":"Delay injection until a clinician can confirm the allergen because early epinephrine is contraindicated in suspected anaphylaxis"}}
questions.rationale: Epinephrine auto-injectors are intended for intramuscular or subcutaneous administration into the anterolateral thigh. Device-specific instructions must be followed because activation and hold times differ among products. Many products permit use through clothing when necessary.
questions.source_name: FDA/Prescribing Information — Epinephrine Auto-Injectors
questions.source_detail: Recommended anterolateral-thigh administration and product-specific instructions

questions.stem: Which statement about home insulin storage is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Unopened insulin is generally refrigerated, while allowable room-temperature storage after opening depends on the specific product label","B":"Insulin should be frozen whenever possible because freezing extends potency beyond the labeled expiration date","C":"Insulin may be stored in direct sunlight as long as the cap remains on the vial or pen","D":"All insulin products have identical room-temperature stability periods, so product-specific labeling does not need to be checked"}}
questions.rationale: FDA notes that manufacturers generally recommend refrigerated storage for insulin and that unopened refrigerated products retain potency to the labeled expiration date. Room-temperature allowances vary by product, so the specific label should be followed; insulin should not be frozen or exposed to excessive heat.
questions.source_name: FDA — Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
questions.source_detail: Refrigerated storage and labeled room-temperature allowances

questions.stem: A chemotherapy drug is classified as a vesicant. What is the key implication if the drug extravasates into surrounding tissue?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It can cause severe local tissue injury, including blistering, ulceration, or necrosis depending on the agent","B":"It causes only transient discomfort because vesicants cannot produce tissue necrosis after extravasation","C":"Its effects are exclusively systemic, so the infusion site does not require assessment during administration","D":"It is interchangeable with a nonvesicant irritant because both terms indicate the same degree of tissue injury"}}
questions.rationale: ONS extravasation guidance identifies extravasation of vesicants or irritants with vesicant properties as a potentially serious event that can cause pain, swelling, erythema and, in severe cases, tissue necrosis and ulceration. This supports option A and distinguishes vesicants from agents without comparable tissue-damaging potential.
questions.source_name: Oncology Nursing Society — Extravasation Management
questions.source_detail: Extravasation Management > Background; last reviewed September 18, 2025: severe extravasation can cause tissue necrosis and ulceration.

questions.stem: A client reports tremor and a rapid heartbeat after using inhaled albuterol. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They are recognized adverse effects of beta-adrenergic agonist therapy and should be assessed for severity and persistence","B":"They prove the medication is ineffective and require the client to double the next dose without further assessment","C":"They are unrelated to albuterol because inhaled beta agonists cannot produce systemic cardiovascular or neuromuscular effects","D":"They always indicate anaphylaxis and therefore establish a diagnosis of severe allergic reaction without other findings"}}
questions.rationale: Current albuterol labeling identifies tachycardia as a common adverse reaction and recognizes cardiovascular effects from beta-adrenergic stimulation; tremor is also a recognized beta-agonist effect. These findings require clinical assessment rather than automatic dose escalation or attribution to anaphylaxis.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Aerosol Prescribing Information
questions.source_detail: Warnings and Precautions 5.4 Cardiovascular Effects; Adverse Reactions 6.1 includes tachycardia; beta-adrenergic stimulation can also produce tremor.

questions.stem: When rotating a client from one opioid to another, what is the purpose of an equianalgesic estimate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"To estimate relative analgesic potency as a starting point, followed by a safety reduction and individualized titration when switching opioids","B":"To establish an exact milligram-for-milligram dose that can be transferred directly between all opioids without adjustment","C":"To eliminate the need to consider incomplete cross-tolerance, organ function, route, or individual response during the switch","D":"To determine only nonopioid analgesic doses because equianalgesic concepts are not used when comparing opioid potency"}}
questions.rationale: Equianalgesic tables estimate relative opioid potency but are not exact conversion targets. When switching to a different opioid, the calculated equivalent is generally reduced to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variability, then titrated to clinical response.
questions.source_name: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — 2022
questions.source_detail: Cautions on opioid conversion and incomplete cross-tolerance

questions.stem: A client is stopping long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy after the prescriber confirms there is no continuing indication. Which teaching is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Transient upper gastrointestinal symptoms can occur from rebound acid hypersecretion after discontinuation","B":"Stopping a PPI permanently suppresses gastric acid, so rebound symptoms cannot occur after discontinuation","C":"A PPI must always be tapered because abrupt discontinuation is prohibited by current expert guidance","D":"Any symptoms after stopping prove that the original diagnosis was incorrect and require permanent PPI therapy"}}
questions.rationale: AGA guidance advises that patients discontinuing long-term PPI therapy may experience transient symptoms from rebound acid hypersecretion. Importantly, either tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered, so the original claim that abrupt cessation itself is inappropriate was too strong.
questions.source_name: American Gastroenterological Association — Clinical Practice Update on De-Prescribing PPIs
questions.source_detail: Rebound acid hypersecretion; tapering or abrupt discontinuation may be considered

questions.stem: A client is about to start atorvastatin. Which liver-related monitoring statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Consider liver-enzyme testing before initiation and repeat testing later when clinically indicated","B":"Routine weekly liver-enzyme testing is required for every client throughout atorvastatin therapy","C":"Liver enzymes should never be checked because atorvastatin has no recognized hepatic adverse effects","D":"Serum calcium is the primary laboratory test used to detect atorvastatin-related hepatic injury"}}
questions.rationale: Current atorvastatin labeling advises considering liver-enzyme testing before initiation and when clinically indicated thereafter. The original item incorrectly implied routine ongoing liver-enzyme monitoring solely because of a family history of liver problems.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — LIPITOR (atorvastatin calcium) Prescribing Information
questions.source_detail: Hepatic dysfunction warning and liver-enzyme testing guidance

questions.stem: A client with heart failure who is receiving high-dose diuretic therapy is starting lisinopril. Which effect requires particularly close monitoring when therapy is initiated?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Symptomatic hypotension, especially when diuresis has contributed to volume or sodium depletion","B":"Marked hypertension because ACE inhibition typically causes an abrupt increase in systemic vascular resistance","C":"Hyperglycemia because severe glucose elevation is the principal first-dose effect of lisinopril","D":"No hemodynamic effect because diuretic therapy eliminates the blood-pressure response to ACE inhibition"}}
questions.rationale: Lisinopril can cause symptomatic hypotension. Labeling identifies heart failure, high-dose diuretic therapy, and severe volume or salt depletion among risk factors for excessive hypotension, so close monitoring is appropriate when therapy is initiated in such patients.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Lisinopril Prescribing Information
questions.source_detail: Hypotension risk with heart failure, high-dose diuretics, and volume/salt depletion

questions.stem: A hospital promotes annual influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel. What is the primary patient-safety rationale?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Vaccination replaces standard precautions and other respiratory infection-control measures during influenza season.","B":"Vaccination eliminates all influenza infections among healthcare personnel and patients during the season.","C":"Vaccination is used mainly to satisfy an administrative requirement unrelated to transmission prevention.","D":"Vaccination reduces influenza illness and the risk that infected healthcare personnel transmit influenza to vulnerable patients."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel as an important infection-prevention measure. Vaccination reduces influenza illness among personnel and helps reduce transmission risk to patients; it complements rather than replaces other infection-control practices.
questions.source_name: CDC — Influenza Vaccination Information for Health Care Workers
questions.source_detail: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for healthcare personnel to protect personnel and patients and reduce healthcare-associated transmission risk.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous exposure to blood from a patient with known hepatitis C virus infection. Which follow-up is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obtain recommended baseline and follow-up HCV testing because no vaccine or recommended HCV postexposure prophylaxis is available.","B":"Give hepatitis C immune globulin immediately and omit follow-up testing if the exposure site was washed promptly.","C":"Administer a hepatitis C vaccine immediately and repeat the vaccine after the occupational-health evaluation is complete.","D":"Start direct-acting antiviral treatment immediately after every exposure without first performing baseline or follow-up testing."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends baseline testing and indicated follow-up testing after occupational HCV exposure. HCV postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended, and there is no HCV vaccine. Detecting acute infection permits referral for treatment.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guidelines for Health Care Personnel Exposed to Hepatitis C Virus
questions.source_detail: Occupational HCV exposure requires baseline/follow-up testing; postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended.

questions.stem: A nurse is responsible for controlled substances on a hospital unit. Which storage practice best supports diversion prevention and accountability?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep controlled substances in an unlocked medication cart when authorized staff remain somewhere on the unit.","B":"Store controlled substances securely with access limited to authorized personnel and maintain required accountability records.","C":"Share medication-storage access credentials among staff so urgent doses can be obtained without individual authentication.","D":"Move controlled substances to an open medication shelf during busy periods and reconcile the inventory at the end of the shift."}}
questions.rationale: Controlled substances require secure storage and access controls appropriate to the setting, together with required records and accountability processes. Leaving them unsecured or sharing access credentials undermines diversion prevention.
questions.source_name: U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration — Controlled Substance Security Requirements
questions.source_detail: Controlled substances must be stored and handled under security controls that guard against theft and diversion, with access limited appropriately.

questions.stem: A client uses supplemental oxygen at home. Which instruction is most important for reducing fire risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep oxygen equipment away from smoking, open flames, sparks, and other ignition sources because oxygen accelerates combustion.","B":"Smoking is acceptable if the nasal cannula is removed briefly because oxygen remaining in clothing and the environment poses no risk.","C":"Place the oxygen concentrator next to a gas stove so the client can observe the equipment while preparing meals.","D":"Use petroleum-based products around oxygen equipment because they reduce static electricity and therefore lower ignition risk."}}
questions.rationale: Oxygen itself is not flammable, but an oxygen-enriched environment allows materials to ignite more readily and burn more intensely. Home oxygen must be kept away from smoking and other ignition sources.
questions.source_name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration — Safe Use of Oxygen Equipment
questions.source_detail: Home oxygen users should avoid smoking, flames, sparks, and other ignition sources around oxygen equipment.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that an electrical medical device has a frayed power cord. What is the appropriate action?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue using the device until the current patient treatment is finished, then report the damaged cord.","B":"Remove the device from service and follow facility procedures for evaluation, repair, or replacement by qualified personnel.","C":"Wrap the damaged section with adhesive tape and return the device to routine patient-care use immediately.","D":"Repair the electrical cord personally if the device still powers on and no exposed conductor is readily visible."}}
questions.rationale: Damaged electrical cords can create shock, fire, and equipment-failure hazards. Unsafe equipment should be removed from service and managed through the organization's maintenance/equipment-safety process rather than improvised at the bedside.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Electrical Safety
questions.source_detail: Damaged electrical equipment and flexible cords must not remain in service when defects could expose users to electrical hazards.

questions.stem: A maternity unit uses matching parent-infant identification bands and additional security controls for newborns. What is the best interpretation of this practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These measures are appropriate only in hospitals located in areas with a documented high rate of violent crime.","B":"These measures are unnecessary because newborn abduction is too rare to warrant prevention procedures in hospitals.","C":"These measures provide layered safeguards against infant misidentification or abduction and supplement routine identification procedures.","D":"Electronic security controls eliminate the need for staff to verify parent-infant identification before releasing a newborn."}}
questions.rationale: Newborn security uses layered safeguards rather than a single control. Matching identification and facility security procedures reduce the risk of wrong-family release and infant abduction; technology does not replace staff verification.
questions.source_name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children — For Healthcare Professionals
questions.source_detail: Healthcare facilities use prevention and response safeguards to reduce infant-abduction risk.

questions.stem: A client self-administers insulin at home. Which instruction about used needles is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place used needles loose in household trash so sanitation workers can identify them during collection.","B":"Flush used needles down the toilet after each injection to prevent accidental contact by household members.","C":"Place used needles promptly in an FDA-cleared sharps container and follow community disposal requirements when the container is ready for disposal.","D":"Store used needles uncovered on a rigid tray until several have accumulated, then transfer them together to the household trash."}}
questions.rationale: FDA recommends placing used sharps immediately into an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container and following local disposal rules. Loose disposal, flushing, or leaving exposed sharps creates preventable needlestick risk.
questions.source_name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration — Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps
questions.source_detail: Used sharps should be placed immediately in FDA-cleared sharps containers and disposed of according to community guidance.

questions.stem: A nurse educator discusses the historical development of universal precautions. Which statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CDC developed universal precautions during the HIV/AIDS era to treat blood and specified body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of known infection status.","B":"Universal precautions originated as a food-safety program and were later adapted to prevent occupational blood exposure in hospitals.","C":"Universal precautions required isolation of every hospitalized patient regardless of diagnosis, symptoms, or anticipated exposure to body fluids.","D":"Universal precautions were designed to replace hand hygiene and personal protective equipment with routine environmental disinfection alone."}}
questions.rationale: CDC's universal precautions approach emerged in the 1980s amid concern about occupational transmission of bloodborne pathogens, particularly HIV and HBV. It treated blood and certain body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of known status and later contributed to Standard Precautions.
questions.source_name: CDC — 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions
questions.source_detail: Historical background describes Universal Precautions as an approach developed for prevention of occupational bloodborne infection and later incorporated into Standard Precautions.

questions.stem: A nurse manager evaluates whether reducing registered-nurse staffing could affect patient safety. Which finding is most consistent with the evidence base?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lower nurse staffing has been associated with worse patient outcomes, including increased adverse events and mortality in multiple observational studies.","B":"Lower nurse staffing consistently improves patient outcomes because fewer handoffs occur between registered nurses during hospitalization.","C":"Nurse staffing affects hospital finances but has not been associated with measurable differences in patient safety or clinical outcomes.","D":"Patient outcomes are independent of nurse staffing as long as the unit maintains the same number of occupied inpatient beds."}}
questions.rationale: A substantial observational evidence base links lower registered-nurse staffing with worse outcomes, including adverse events and mortality. The evidence supports staffing as a patient-safety factor, although individual studies do not establish that staffing is the sole cause of every outcome.
questions.source_name: AHRQ Patient Safety Network — Nursing and Patient Safety
questions.source_detail: Evidence reviews associate nurse staffing and workload with patient safety outcomes, including mortality and adverse events.

questions.stem: A nurse applies transcultural nursing principles when planning care for a client whose cultural background differs from the nurse's. Which action best reflects this approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the same care plan for every client because modifying care for cultural preferences creates inconsistent nursing standards.","B":"Base the plan on assumptions about the client's cultural group without asking the individual client about preferences or practices.","C":"Exclude cultural practices from the plan whenever biomedical treatment is available, even when the practices do not conflict with safety.","D":"Assess the client's individual cultural values and practices and incorporate relevant preferences into safe, clinically appropriate care."}}
questions.rationale: Culturally congruent nursing care requires individualized assessment rather than stereotyping. Relevant cultural values, beliefs, and practices can be incorporated into care when compatible with patient safety and clinical needs.
questions.source_name: HHS Office of Minority Health — National CLAS Standards
questions.source_detail: Culturally and linguistically appropriate services call for respectful, responsive care that addresses individual cultural health beliefs and practices.

questions.stem: A nurse manager uses a servant-leadership approach. Which behavior best reflects this leadership style?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Centralizing authority so staff members have little opportunity to develop autonomy or leadership capacity.","B":"Prioritizing the leader's status and recognition when those goals conflict with the growth of team members.","C":"Avoiding difficult decisions so responsibility for team outcomes rests entirely with frontline staff.","D":"Supporting the growth, development, and needs of team members while remaining accountable for leadership decisions and outcomes."}}
questions.rationale: The Open RN Nursing Management and Professional Concepts text describes servant leadership as focusing on the growth and well-being of team members, sharing in decision-making, and developing team members to their highest potential. This does not imply absent or avoidant leadership.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Management and Professional Concepts, 2nd ed.
questions.source_detail: Chapter 4 Leadership and Management, Table 4.2b Characteristics of Leadership Styles — Servant: focus on growth and well-being of team members, shared decision-making, development to highest potential.

questions.stem: A new nurse reports repeated belittling comments, social exclusion, and intimidation from a colleague. How should the charge nurse interpret this behavior?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"As workplace bullying or lateral violence that should be addressed through organizational safety and reporting processes.","B":"As a normal socialization practice that new nurses should tolerate until they become established on the unit.","C":"As a private interpersonal issue with no recognized relationship to staff well-being, retention, or patient safety.","D":"As conduct that should be ignored unless physical injury occurs because verbal and relational aggression are not workplace-safety concerns."}}
questions.rationale: ANA identifies incivility, bullying, lateral violence, and workplace violence as serious organizational and professional concerns. Repeated belittling, intimidation, and exclusion should not be normalized as part of nursing socialization and should be addressed through established reporting and prevention processes.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Workplace Violence Position Statement
questions.source_detail: ANA recognizes bullying, incivility, and lateral violence as threats to a respectful and safe nursing work environment and calls for organizational prevention, reporting, investigation, and response.

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains the difference between a preceptor and a mentor. Which description best fits a preceptor?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A clinician assigned to provide structured, role-specific orientation, supervision, feedback, and skill development for a defined period.","B":"A person whose only function is long-term informal career advice without responsibility for clinical orientation or competency development.","C":"A role that is interchangeable with mentoring because preceptorship has no defined educational or clinical purpose.","D":"A manager who performs formal disciplinary evaluation but does not support transition into a clinical role or practice setting."}}
questions.rationale: Open RN describes orientation as competency-based and typically time-limited, with a novice nurse working with a preceptor. Preceptors are experienced nurses who serve as role models and resources, coach the new nurse into the role, evaluate performance, and provide feedback.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Health Alterations: Transition to Practice
questions.source_detail: Chapter 12.5 Transitioning to the PN Role > Orientation and Preceptors: orientation is competency-based; preceptors coach, evaluate performance, and provide feedback.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes continuous quality improvement in healthcare?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It is an ongoing process of measuring performance, learning from results, testing changes, and improving systems rather than merely confirming minimum compliance.","B":"It is limited to determining whether a fixed standard was met and ends once the organization demonstrates compliance.","C":"It focuses primarily on assigning individual blame after an adverse event instead of improving the processes that shape performance.","D":"It is unrelated to routine clinical operations because quality improvement is performed only during external accreditation surveys."}}
questions.rationale: IHI describes quality improvement as a systematic, learning-oriented approach to improving performance and redesigning processes. Modern quality management integrates planning, control, and continuous improvement rather than relying only on reactive compliance checks.
questions.source_name: Institute for Healthcare Improvement — Whole System Quality
questions.source_detail: IHI describes quality improvement as part of a continuous learning system that integrates quality planning, quality control, and improvement activities.

questions.stem: A client with decision-making capacity says the current care plan does not reflect the client's goals. The nurse raises the concern during the interprofessional discussion. Which nursing role is demonstrated?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Patient advocacy, because the nurse is helping protect the client's rights, preferences, and informed participation in care.","B":"Boundary violation, because nurses should not communicate a capable client's expressed goals to other members of the healthcare team.","C":"Unauthorized prescribing, because discussing the client's goals is equivalent to independently changing the medical treatment plan.","D":"Case management only, because advocacy for a client's wishes is not part of professional nursing ethics or practice."}}
questions.rationale: Advocacy is a core nursing responsibility. ANA ethical guidance supports nurses in protecting patients' rights, promoting informed decision-making, and communicating patient preferences within the healthcare team.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Code of Ethics for Nurses / Patient Advocacy
questions.source_detail: ANA ethical standards identify advocacy for patient health, safety, rights, preferences, and informed decision-making as a professional nursing responsibility.

questions.stem: A client with decision-making capacity refuses a recommended treatment after receiving information about the proposed treatment, expected benefits, material risks, and alternatives. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Respect the refusal, document the relevant education and the client's decision according to policy, and communicate the refusal to the appropriate clinician or team.","B":"Document only the words 'client refused' because information provided before the refusal has no relevance to the clinical record.","C":"Proceed with the treatment because a capable patient's refusal becomes invalid whenever clinicians believe the treatment is beneficial.","D":"Ask a family member to override the client's decision because informed refusal applies only when the healthcare team agrees with the patient's choice."}}
questions.rationale: A patient with decision-making capacity has the right to withhold informed consent. Safe practice includes respecting the decision, documenting the refusal and relevant information provided according to organizational policy, and communicating the decision to the responsible clinical team. The original item was narrowed to avoid claiming a single universal documentation formula for every jurisdiction and setting.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Performance Goal: Safe Informed Care
questions.source_detail: Joint Commission patient-rights standards require respect for the patient's right to give or withhold informed consent and communication in a manner the patient can understand.

questions.stem: A client with asthma asks which exposures can trigger symptoms. Which response is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Triggers can include respiratory viral infections, tobacco smoke, cold air, exercise, and relevant allergens, although individual triggers vary.","B":"Food exposure is the only recognized trigger category, so environmental and respiratory exposures do not need to be considered.","C":"Exercise is the only predictable trigger, and viral infections, smoke, allergens, and weather changes do not affect asthma symptoms.","D":"Asthma symptoms occur independently of identifiable exposures, so identifying and reducing individual triggers is not useful."}}
questions.rationale: GINA identifies multiple common asthma triggers, including viral respiratory infections, tobacco smoke, cold air or weather changes, exercise, and allergens in susceptible individuals. Trigger profiles vary, so teaching should be individualized rather than implying every patient reacts to every exposure.
questions.source_name: Global Initiative for Asthma — Asthma Triggers
questions.source_detail: GINA identifies cold air, viral respiratory infection, tobacco smoke, exercise, and allergens among common triggers, with individual variation.

questions.stem: Which finding is classically associated with the chronic bronchitis phenotype of COPD rather than emphysema?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Chronic cough with sputum production; the traditional epidemiologic definition is cough and sputum for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.","B":"Destruction of alveolar walls and enlargement of distal air spaces as the defining pathologic abnormality of the chronic bronchitis phenotype.","C":"Absence of cough and sputum because mucus hypersecretion is not associated with chronic bronchitis in patients with COPD.","D":"A disease pattern unrelated to tobacco exposure or other inhaled irritants, because airway inflammation is not involved in chronic bronchitis."}}
questions.rationale: GOLD retains chronic bronchitis as a clinically and epidemiologically useful term defined by cough and sputum production for at least 3 months in each of two consecutive years, while emphysema refers to destruction of gas-exchanging lung surfaces. The phenotypes can overlap and are not synonymous with COPD as a whole.
questions.source_name: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease — 2026 GOLD Report
questions.source_detail: 2026 GOLD Report / Digital GOLD Report, COPD definition discussion: chronic bronchitis is cough and sputum production for at least 3 months in each of two consecutive years; emphysema is destruction of gas-exchanging surfaces.

questions.stem: A client develops reproducible calf discomfort while walking that resolves after several minutes of rest. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Intermittent claudication associated with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease and impaired blood flow during exertion.","B":"A normal consequence of aging that does not warrant vascular assessment when the pain consistently resolves with rest.","C":"Deep vein thrombosis, which is characteristically defined by reproducible exertional pain that disappears promptly with rest.","D":"Restless legs syndrome, which typically produces the same predictable exertional ischemic pain pattern during walking."}}
questions.rationale: The AHA describes intermittent claudication as lower-extremity discomfort provoked by walking or exercise and relieved by rest. This is a classic symptom of peripheral artery disease and should not be dismissed as normal aging.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — Symptoms of Peripheral Artery Disease
questions.source_detail: AHA describes intermittent claudication as leg discomfort during activity that improves after stopping and resting.

questions.stem: A client has chronic lower-leg swelling, aching and heaviness, varicose veins, and skin changes that become more noticeable after prolonged standing and improve with leg elevation. Which condition best matches this pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Chronic venous insufficiency caused by impaired venous return and venous hypertension in the lower extremities.","B":"Lower-extremity arterial insufficiency, whose classic exertional ischemic pattern is better characterized by claudication relieved by rest.","C":"An uncomplicated musculoskeletal disorder, because edema, varicosities, and stasis-related skin changes do not indicate venous disease.","D":"A normal age-related finding that requires no vascular assessment even when progressive edema and skin changes are present."}}
questions.rationale: The Society for Vascular Surgery describes chronic venous insufficiency as impaired venous return with symptoms such as leg or ankle swelling, aching or heaviness, varicose veins, and skin changes. Symptoms often worsen with prolonged standing and may improve with elevation or compression. This pattern differs from classic arterial claudication.
questions.source_name: Society for Vascular Surgery — Chronic Venous Insufficiency
questions.source_detail: CVI commonly causes swelling, heaviness, discomfort, varicose veins and skin changes; prolonged standing worsens symptoms and leg elevation can provide relief.

questions.stem: A client has symmetric pain and swelling in both hands with prolonged morning stiffness. Which finding is more characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis than osteoarthritis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Pain mainly with joint use, brief stiffness after rest, and no persistent inflammatory pattern","B":"Symmetric small-joint inflammation, prolonged morning stiffness, and possible systemic symptoms","C":"Pain limited to weight-bearing joints, brief morning stiffness, and a mainly degenerative pattern","D":"Joint disease confined to older adults, without autoimmune inflammation or extra-articular features"}}
questions.rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease. It commonly affects small joints of the hands and feet in a symmetric pattern and may cause prolonged morning stiffness, fatigue, and low-grade fever. Osteoarthritis is primarily degenerative and is more commonly associated with pain related to joint use and shorter periods of morning stiffness.
questions.source_name: NIAMS — Rheumatoid Arthritis
questions.source_detail: Symptoms of Rheumatoid Arthritis: symmetric pattern; morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes; fatigue and occasional fever. Last reviewed by NIAMS current page accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with an acute gout flare in the great toe is prescribed colchicine. Which explanation of colchicine is most accurate for the current flare?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals during an acute gout flare today","B":"Directly dissolves deposited urate crystals and permanently lowers the serum urate level","C":"Serves as the primary urate-lowering drug used to maintain serum urate below target long term","D":"Treats the flare by eradicating a bacterial infection within the affected joint tissues"}}
questions.rationale: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory treatment used for gout flares. It does not directly dissolve urate crystals or serve as a urate-lowering therapy. Importantly, colchicine can also be used as anti-inflammatory prophylaxis when urate-lowering therapy is initiated, so the prior wording that implied it has no preventive role was removed.
questions.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — 2020 Guideline for the Management of Gout
questions.source_detail: 2020 ACR Gout Guideline: colchicine is an accepted first-line anti-inflammatory option for gout flares; anti-inflammatory prophylaxis such as colchicine is recommended when initiating urate-lowering therapy for at least 3–6 months.

questions.stem: A client reports months of widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep, and difficulty concentrating. No alternative inflammatory or structural diagnosis has been identified. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fibromyalgia, which commonly causes widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep, and cognitive symptoms","B":"Rheumatoid arthritis, which is defined by the absence of inflammatory or joint abnormalities","C":"Normal aging, in which persistent widespread pain and cognitive symptoms are expected findings","D":"An acute infection, which typically causes months of stable widespread pain without other changes"}}
questions.rationale: Fibromyalgia is a chronic disorder characterized by widespread pain and commonly includes fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive difficulty. There is no specific laboratory or imaging test that confirms fibromyalgia; testing may be used to evaluate for other causes. The earlier wording was tightened so that normal inflammatory markers or imaging are not presented as diagnostic criteria by themselves.
questions.source_name: NIAMS — Fibromyalgia
questions.source_detail: NIAMS overview and diagnosis pages: chronic widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and cognitive difficulties are common; there is no specific laboratory or imaging test for fibromyalgia. Last reviewed May 2024; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client for possible Parkinson disease. Which finding is most consistent with the core motor syndrome?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bradykinesia with resting tremor and/or rigidity developing as a progressive motor syndrome","B":"Ascending weakness with rapid progression and spontaneous resolution over several hours","C":"Isolated cognitive decline without bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, or other motor findings","D":"Sudden episodic weakness with complete recovery and no progressive movement abnormality"}}
questions.rationale: Parkinson disease is characterized clinically by bradykinesia together with other parkinsonian motor features such as resting tremor or rigidity. Symptoms usually develop gradually rather than as abrupt, fully resolving neurologic episodes.
questions.source_name: NINDS — Parkinson's Disease
questions.source_detail: NINDS Parkinson disease overview: motor manifestations include resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia; Parkinson disease is progressive. Accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client receiving lithium maintenance therapy for bipolar I disorder has a properly timed serum lithium concentration of 0.9 mEq/L and no symptoms of toxicity. How should the nurse interpret this result?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Below the usual maintenance target and evidence that lithium treatment is not effective clinically","B":"Within the labeled maintenance target and interpreted together with the clinical response","C":"Above the toxic threshold and an indication for immediate emergency dialysis treatment now","D":"Unrelated to lithium dosing and therefore unnecessary for ongoing medication monitoring"}}
questions.rationale: Current lithium labeling targets a serum concentration of 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L for maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder. A level of 0.9 mEq/L is therefore within the labeled maintenance target, but dosing decisions still require clinical correlation and ongoing monitoring.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Lithium Carbonate prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Dosage and Administration, maintenance treatment: target serum lithium concentration 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L; serum concentration monitoring required.

questions.stem: A client taking digoxin has a serum digoxin concentration of 1.5 ng/mL drawn at least 6 hours after the last dose. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Proof of digoxin toxicity that requires immediate antidote treatment regardless of other findings","B":"Too low to produce a therapeutic effect and therefore an automatic indication to increase the dose","C":"A value interpreted with symptoms, renal function, electrolytes, and the overall clinical response","D":"A result whose timing after the last dose has no effect on how the concentration is interpreted"}}
questions.rationale: Digoxin labeling states that concentrations below 0.5 ng/mL have been associated with diminished efficacy and concentrations above 2 ng/mL with increased toxicity without increased benefit. It also specifically warns not to use an isolated serum concentration alone to increase or decrease the dose. A level of 1.5 ng/mL therefore requires clinical interpretation rather than being automatically labeled therapeutic or toxic.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Digoxin prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Section 2.5 Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels: interpret serum concentration in the overall clinical context; sample just before the next dose or at least 6 hours after the last dose.

questions.stem: A client taking phenobarbital for seizure control asks whether a serum drug concentration can replace keeping a record of seizure frequency and adverse effects. Which response is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No; a serum concentration cannot replace monitoring of seizure frequency and adverse effects","B":"No; the level supports dosing assessment but must be interpreted with seizure control and adverse effects","C":"Yes; phenobarbital concentration testing is used only to evaluate renal function during treatment","D":"No; phenobarbital serum concentrations have no useful role in anticonvulsant medication management"}}
questions.rationale: Phenobarbital labeling recognizes serum anticonvulsant levels as part of dose assessment and directs clinicians to use laboratory reference values. Drug levels do not replace assessment of clinical seizure control, adherence, sedation, or toxicity.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Phenobarbital Tablets prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Dosage and Administration, Anticonvulsant Use: clinical laboratory reference values should be used to determine therapeutic anticonvulsant serum levels; dosing also depends on patient age, weight, and condition.

questions.stem: A client taking carbamazepine develops new dizziness, diplopia, and unsteady coordination. What is the nurse's best interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recognized neurologic adverse effects that warrant prompt medication-safety evaluation","B":"Expected evidence of improved seizure control that requires no additional assessment","C":"Findings unrelated to carbamazepine because the drug does not affect vision or coordination","D":"Evidence of an ear disorder that should be treated without reviewing the medication regimen"}}
questions.rationale: Carbamazepine labeling lists dizziness, disturbances of coordination, blurred vision, and transient diplopia among nervous-system adverse reactions. New neurologic symptoms should prompt medication-safety assessment rather than being assumed to represent improved seizure control.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Carbamazepine prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Adverse Reactions, Nervous System: dizziness, disturbances of coordination, blurred vision, transient diplopia and related neurologic effects.

questions.stem: An insulin-treated adult has an uncertain diabetes classification, and the clinician orders C-peptide with a concurrent glucose level. What information can this test contribute?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Endogenous insulin secretion, which can help clarify diabetes classification in the clinical context","B":"Average blood glucose over roughly three months, which is measured using hemoglobin A1c testing","C":"Kidney filtration alone, without clinically meaningful information about pancreatic insulin secretion","D":"Diabetes type by itself, regardless of insulin use, concurrent glucose, or a recent emergency"}}
questions.rationale: ADA Standards of Care 2026 describe C-peptide as a classification aid in insulin-treated people. Interpretation requires context, including concurrent glucose, and C-peptide should not be tested within 2 weeks of a hyperglycemic emergency. It reflects endogenous beta-cell insulin secretion but does not independently classify every person with diabetes.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026
questions.source_detail: Section 2, Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes, classification flowchart footnote 4: C-peptide is indicated in insulin-treated people for classification; interpret with concurrent glucose and avoid testing within 2 weeks of a hyperglycemic emergency.

questions.stem: A client presents with dyspnea and has a markedly elevated BNP concentration. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Possible heart failure, while recognizing that other clinical conditions can also affect BNP concentrations","B":"A pulmonary cause of dyspnea, because an elevated BNP specifically excludes underlying cardiac disease","C":"Normal cardiac function, because BNP rises only when the lungs are the primary source of symptoms","D":"No useful information, because BNP has no established role in evaluating otherwise unexplained dyspnea"}}
questions.rationale: Natriuretic peptide testing is used to support the diagnosis or exclusion of heart failure in patients presenting with dyspnea, but BNP is not a stand-alone diagnosis. Age, kidney function, atrial fibrillation, obesity, and other clinical factors can influence levels, so the result requires clinical correlation.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
questions.source_detail: Biomarkers section: in patients presenting with dyspnea, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP is useful to support diagnosis or exclusion of heart failure; interpretation remains clinical.

questions.stem: Which technique should a client use when instilling prescribed eye drops?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Pull down the lower lid, place the drop in the conjunctival pocket, and avoid touching the bottle tip","B":"Touch the bottle tip to the cornea so medication is delivered directly to the intended eye surface","C":"Close the eye tightly and rub vigorously after each drop to improve medication absorption in the eye","D":"Place the medication on the closed eyelid and wait for it to enter when the eye is opened again"}}
questions.rationale: The National Eye Institute instructs patients to pull the lower eyelid down to create a pocket, place the prescribed drop into that pocket, and keep the bottle tip from touching the eye or eyelid to reduce contamination and injury risk.
questions.source_name: National Eye Institute — How to Put in Eye Drops
questions.source_detail: Use eye drops correctly; prevent infections when using eye drops. Updated December 5, 2024.

questions.stem: A nurse is immobilizing a suspected forearm fracture before transport. Which action is essential after applying the splint?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assess distal circulation, sensation, and movement after splinting and respond to any compromise","B":"Tighten the splint until distal pulses are difficult to feel so the fracture cannot move","C":"Remove the splint repeatedly to test movement at the injured area during patient transport","D":"Ignore increasing numbness or tingling if the limb remains externally aligned in the splint"}}
questions.rationale: A splint is intended to limit movement and protect injured tissue, but it must not impair circulation or nerve function. Distal neurovascular status should be checked after immobilization, and excessive compression requires correction. The prior item overemphasized a generalized 'joint above and below' rule without a sufficiently specific source locator.
questions.source_name: NIAMS — Sports Injuries: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
questions.source_detail: Treatment for serious injuries: immobilization limits movement and reduces pain/swelling; splints, braces and casts support and protect injured bones and soft tissue. Compression should not be tight enough to cut off circulation.

questions.stem: A client has a minor acute ankle sprain with swelling. Which home-care instruction about cold therapy is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a wrapped cold pack for short intervals, such as about 20 minutes, during the acute period","B":"Apply a heating pad immediately after injury because heat reliably reduces acute swelling","C":"Place ice directly on bare skin for prolonged periods to maximize the anti-inflammatory effect","D":"Avoid protection and cold therapy because swelling should be encouraged during early healing"}}
questions.rationale: NIAMS recommends ice for minor acute sports injuries to reduce pain and inflammation, applied for about 20 minutes at a time with a barrier to avoid cold injury. It also advises against immediate heat because heat can increase inflammation and swelling.
questions.source_name: NIAMS — Sports Injuries: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
questions.source_detail: Treatment of minor injuries, R-I-C-E: ice for 20 minutes at a time; do not use heat immediately after injury because it tends to increase inflammation and swelling.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease asks whether everyone with CKD should follow the same low-potassium, low-phosphorus, high-protein diet. Which response is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Individualize sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid goals to stage, labs, and treatment status","B":"Restrict all potassium and phosphorus for every person with CKD regardless of current laboratory values","C":"Substantially increase protein for every person with CKD, including those who are not receiving dialysis","D":"Use no nutrition modifications because dietary intake has no meaningful role in ongoing CKD management"}}
questions.rationale: The National Kidney Foundation emphasizes that there is no single kidney diet for everyone. Sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid targets depend on CKD stage, laboratory values, dialysis status, medications, comorbidities, and individual nutrition needs.
questions.source_name: National Kidney Foundation — Creating a Kidney Friendly Plate
questions.source_detail: Updated June 5, 2026: no single kidney diet works for everyone; food plan changes with CKD stage, labs, dialysis status and other health needs; protein, potassium and phosphorus targets are individualized.

questions.stem: Which screening approach is recommended by the USPSTF for an otherwise eligible woman age 65 years or older without known osteoporosis or a prior fragility fracture?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Screen with DXA bone mineral density, with or without a validated fracture-risk assessment","B":"Screen with a serum calcium level alone because blood testing directly measures bone density","C":"Screen with a routine hip radiograph because standard X-rays detect osteoporosis reliably","D":"Defer screening until a fragility fracture occurs because earlier testing has no proven role"}}
questions.rationale: The USPSTF 2025 recommendation advises screening women 65 years or older for osteoporosis. Screening includes DXA bone mineral density, with or without fracture-risk assessment. Serum calcium and routine radiography are not substitutes for osteoporosis screening.
questions.source_name: USPSTF — Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: Screening
questions.source_detail: Final recommendation January 14, 2025; implementation: screen women age 65 years or older with DXA BMD, with or without fracture-risk assessment.

questions.stem: Why is glaucoma screening with a comprehensive dilated eye examination particularly important for people at increased risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Glaucoma usually causes obvious eye pain before optic-nerve damage or visual field loss develops","B":"Glaucoma often has no early symptoms, and vision loss may be irreversible once it has occurred","C":"Glaucoma is reliably diagnosed by a routine blood test before structural eye changes develop","D":"Glaucoma affects only people who already have severe central vision loss at first presentation"}}
questions.rationale: The National Eye Institute states that glaucoma often has no symptoms at first. A comprehensive dilated eye examination is used to detect glaucoma, and early treatment can help prevent further irreversible vision loss.
questions.source_name: National Eye Institute — Glaucoma
questions.source_detail: Updated 2025-2026 content: early symptoms often none; diagnosis includes comprehensive dilated eye examination; early treatment can protect vision.

questions.stem: An older adult has declining vision and slowed reaction time and asks whether age alone means driving must stop immediately. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assess driving-related function and discuss referral for a formal driving evaluation when indicated","B":"Recommend stopping driving solely because of age, without assessing vision, cognition, or motor skills","C":"Ignore changes in vision or reaction time because clinicians have no role in driving-safety counseling","D":"Treat one abnormal office measure as conclusive proof that the person cannot drive safely"}}
questions.rationale: NHTSA guidance for clinicians supports individualized assessment of driving-related vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function and counseling or referral when concerns are identified. Chronological age alone is not an adequate determination of driving fitness.
questions.source_name: NHTSA — Clinician's Guide to Assessing and Counseling Older Drivers
questions.source_detail: NHTSA older-driver guidance: clinical assessment of driving-related skills evaluates vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function and supports individualized counseling and referral.

questions.stem: A client spends several hours each day performing repetitive handwashing rituals in response to intrusive contamination fears and experiences marked distress when unable to complete them. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with obsessions and compulsions that are distressing and time-consuming","B":"Social anxiety disorder, with fear of scrutiny rather than rituals performed in response to obsessions","C":"Body dysmorphic disorder, with appearance preoccupation rather than contamination-driven rituals","D":"Generalized anxiety disorder, with broad worry rather than repetitive compulsions tied to obsessions"}}
questions.rationale: OCD involves recurring intrusive thoughts or urges and repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response. NIMH specifically lists excessive cleaning or handwashing as a common compulsion and notes that clinically significant symptoms are time-consuming, distressing, or impairing.
questions.source_name: NIMH — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: When Unwanted Thoughts or Repetitive Behaviors Take Over
questions.source_detail: Signs and symptoms: obsessions and compulsions; excessive cleaning or handwashing; symptoms commonly consume more than 1 hour daily or cause significant distress/interference.

questions.stem: A client is preoccupied with a slight or unnoticeable perceived flaw in appearance, repeatedly checks mirrors and seeks reassurance, and has substantial social impairment. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Body dysmorphic disorder, involving appearance preoccupation plus repetitive checking or reassurance","B":"Obsessive-compulsive disorder, involving obsessions and compulsions not centered on appearance flaws","C":"Social anxiety disorder, involving fear of scrutiny rather than persistent perceived appearance defects","D":"Illness anxiety disorder, involving fear of serious disease rather than a perceived appearance flaw"}}
questions.rationale: The American Psychiatric Association describes body dysmorphic disorder as preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws that are not noticeable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking or reassurance seeking and clinically significant distress or impairment.
questions.source_name: American Psychiatric Association — Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
questions.source_detail: Body Dysmorphic Disorder section: perceived flaws not noticeable or slight to others; repetitive mirror checking/reassurance seeking; significant distress or functional impairment.
